lessons.title: ਨਾਂ (nāṁ) — "name," a word older than Europe

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: The first word of the introduction — and one of the clearest bridges between India and Europe.
ਨ (na) + ਾ (the kannā, long-ā sign) + ਂ (the bindi, a nasal dot) becomes ਨਾਂ (nāṁ). A single nasalised syllable.

ਨਾਂ (nāṁ, "name") from Sanskrit ਨਾਮਨ੍ (nāman), from Proto-Indo-European h₃nómn (with a syllabic final n) — the same ancient root as English name, Latin nōmen (English noun, nominate), and Greek onoma. So Punjabi nāṁ and English name are cousins from before either language existed. (The Hindi form is nām; Punjabi nasalises the ending to nāṁ.)

segments.instruction: "nāṁ"
the family — nāṁ / English name / Latin nōmen / Greek onoma

segments.text: The little word that makes the name yours.
ਮ (ma) + ੇ (the lāvā̃, e-sign) becomes ਮੇ (me); ਰ (ra) + ਾ (long ā) becomes ਰਾ (rā). Read ਮੇ, ਰਾ becomes merā.

ਮੇਰਾ (merā, "my") is on the first-person root ma- — the same ma-/me- behind English me, my, mine and Latin meus, and the same root as Hindi merā. The Punjabi "my" and the English "my" are, at the root, one word.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: "my" agrees with the noun

segments.text: Punjabi possessives change to match what is owned: ਮੇਰਾ (merā, masculine), ਮੇਰੀ (merī, feminine), ਮੇਰੇ (mere, plural). nāṁ ("name") is masculine, so it takes merā: merā nāṁ. (You will meet merī the first time you own a feminine noun.)

segments.instruction: "merā"
the m- family — merā (my), English me, my
the feminine form (merī)

segments.text: What root links merā and English my, and what is its feminine form? (The first-person ma-; merī.)

segments.prompt: You hear merā nāṁ. Which word means my?

feedback.correct: Right: merā means my before the masculine noun nāṁ.
feedback.incorrect: The phrase is merā nāṁ: merā means my.

segments.text: The little verb "is" — the same "is" spoken from Ireland to India.
ਹ (ha) + ੈ (the dulāvā̃, ai-sign) becomes ਹੈ (hai). One syllable.

ਹੈ (hai, "is") from Sanskrit ਅਸ੍ਤਿ (asti, "is"), from Proto-Indo-European h₁es- — the root of "to be" across the whole family: English is, German ist, Latin est, Spanish es. Punjabi hai is the Indian cousin of the same tiny verb.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the verb comes last

segments.text: Punjabi is subject–object–verb: "my name Arun is." hai sits at the end of the sentence, where English puts "is" in the middle. Bank the shape — in Punjabi the verb waits until the end.

segments.instruction: "hai"
the family — hai / is / ist / est / es
"merā nāṁ Arun hai" — note hai at the end
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "merā nāṁ Arun hai" — note *hai* at the end]

segments.text: What root is hai from, and where does the verb sit in a Punjabi sentence? (Sanskrit asti / PIE h₁es-; at the end.)

segments.prompt: Complete merā nāṁ Arun... and say where Punjabi puts this verb.

feedback.correct: Right: hai means is and waits at the end.
feedback.incorrect: Use hai, is; Punjabi places the verb at the end.

lessons.title: ਮੇਰਾ ਨਾਂ … ਹੈ (merā nāṁ … hai) — "my name is…"

segments.text: Three atoms you now own, assembled into a first sentence.
ਮੇਰਾ (my) + ਨਾਂ (name) + your name + ਹੈ (is) = merā nāṁ … hai, "my name is…" Merā nāṁ Arun hai. becomes "My name is Arun."

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the verb goes last

segments.text: Punjabi is a subject–object–verb language — literally "my name Arun is." The hai sits at the end, where English puts "is" in the middle. Bank this shape: in Punjabi, the verb waits until the end of the sentence.

lessons.title: ਤੂੰ / ਤੁਸੀਂ (tū̃ / tusī̃) — "you," familiar and respectful

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: To ask a name you need "you" — and Punjabi grades respect the way French does.
ਤੂੰ: ਤ (ta) + ੂ (long ū) + ਂ (nasal bindi) becomes tū̃. ਤੁਸੀਂ: tu + sī̃, a longer, plural-shaped word.

ਤੂੰ (tū̃, familiar "you") from Sanskrit tvam, from PIE tū — the same root as English archaic thou, Latin tū, French tu. ਤੁਸੀਂ (tusī̃, respectful "you") is grammatically plural — the same courtesy-by-plural used by French vous and Hindi āp.
ਤੂੰ (tū̃) — familiar: friends, children, intimates.
ਤੁਸੀਂ (tusī̃) — respectful: elders, strangers, politeness (and true plural, "you all").
For a first meeting, always ਤੁਸੀਂ. Respect takes the plural verb, exactly as in the Romance and other Indo-Aryan tracks.

segments.instruction: "tū̃" (familiar) and "tusī̃" (respectful)
the English cousin of tū̃ (thou)
which you use on first meeting (tusī̃)
segments.source: [YOU SAY: which you use on first meeting (*tusī̃*)]

segments.text: Which "you" is respectful, and what English word is tū̃ cousin to? (Tusī̃; archaic thou, from PIE tū.)

segments.prompt: Which Punjabi you belongs in a first meeting: tū̃ or tusī̃?

feedback.correct: Right: tusī̃ is the respectful first-meeting choice.
feedback.incorrect: Use plural-shaped tusī̃ with elders and strangers.

segments.text: The question-word — and it starts with the k- that heads nearly every Punjabi question.
ਕ (ka) + ੀ (the bihārī, long-ī sign) becomes ਕੀ (kī).

ਕੀ (kī, "what") from Sanskrit kim / the interrogative stem ka-, from PIE kʷo- — the same question-root behind English wh- words (what, who, which) and Latin qu-. Punjabi's question-words nearly all begin with this k-: kī (what), kauṇ (who), kad (when), kithē (where), kivēṁ (how). Learn the k- and you can hear a question coming.

lessons.title: ਤੁਹਾਡਾ ਨਾਂ ਕੀ ਹੈ? (tuhāḍā nāṁ kī hai?) — "what's your name?"

segments.text: Turn the introduction around — ask, instead of tell.

ਤੁਹਾਡਾ (tuhāḍā, "your," the respectful possessive from tusī̃) + ਨਾਂ (nāṁ) (name) + ਕੀ (what) + ਹੈ (hai) (is) becomes literally "your name what is?" Punjabi keeps the verb last again, and simply drops the question-word kī into the object slot.
Answer it with the sentence you built: Merā nāṁ Arun hai. The familiar version swaps tuhāḍā for ਤੇਰਾ (terā, "your," from tū̃): terā nāṁ kī hai?

segments.instruction: the respectful question — tuhāḍā nāṁ kī hai?
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the respectful question — *tuhāḍā nāṁ kī hai?*]

segments.instruction: answer it — merā nāṁ … hai
the familiar "your" (terā)

segments.text: Ask someone's name respectfully, and note where the verb sits. (Tuhāḍā nāṁ kī hai?; the verb is last.)

segments.prompt: Ask what is your name respectfully in Punjabi, then type the romanized question you said.

feedback.correct: Right: tuhāḍā nāṁ kī hai, with hai last.
feedback.incorrect: Use respectful tuhāḍā, then nāṁ, kī, and final hai.

lessons.title: ਖ਼ੁਸ਼ੀ ਹੋਈ (khushī hoī) — "pleased to meet you"
lessons.gloss: pleased to meet you — literally happiness happened

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: The warm close of an introduction — and, like shukrīā, it comes from Persian, not Sanskrit.
ਖ਼ੁਸ਼ੀ (khushī): note two pair bindis (dots beneath) — ਖ਼ (kh) and ਸ਼ (sh) — both marking Perso-Arabic sounds, exactly as you saw on ਸ਼ in shukrīā (Chapter 1).

The Punjabi "pleased to meet you" is ਤੁਹਾਨੂੰ ਮਿਲ ਕੇ ਖ਼ੁਸ਼ੀ ਹੋਈ (tuhānū̃ mil ke khushī hoī) — literally "having met you, happiness happened." The key word ਖ਼ੁਸ਼ੀ (khushī, "happiness") is not Sanskrit — it is Persian (khush, "happy, pleasant"), one of the thousands of Persian words woven through Punjabi. So even introducing yourself draws on Punjabi's two vocabularies: Sanskrit (nāṁ, hai) and Perso-Arabic (khushī) — the thread you first met in Chapter 1's shukrīā.

kī from ka- becomes English what; tū̃ from tū becomes thou.
